problem: Recent neural navigation architectures are too slow and noise-sensitive for real robots (Habitat Challenge 2020 agents mostly failed under simultaneous sensor and actuator noise), and object-goal navigation with sparse rewards learns slowly over long horizons.
motivation: Real robots have noisy cameras and actuators and limited onboard compute, so a real-time, noise-robust pipeline that can be pre-trained in simulation (sim2real) is needed. The authors combine fast instance segmentation, SLAM with known control commands, and hierarchical RL that avoids hand-crafted rewards.
key_idea: Combine real-time instance segmentation, control-aware visual SLAM (a motion model built from the known action matrices) and a two-level hierarchical RL agent (TD3 subgoals over a DDDQN low-level policy, trained with hindsight transitions) into one framework, HISNav, trained in Habitat.
insight: Replacing the constant-velocity motion model with the expected displacement of the executed action improves SLAM accuracy and speeds up keypoint matching (Tables 3 and 5), which makes 10 Hz real-time operation possible. The hierarchical hindsight RL reaches SPL 0.6 on noisy point-goal navigation about twice as fast as PPO or RND (3M vs 6M steps), but the object-navigation quality is admittedly still low and was only tested on a single scene.
method: HISNav Dataset: 135,962 Habitat/Matterport3D RGB-D frames from 49 scenes, with instance labels for 40 classes, GT poses (TUM format) and control matrices, under 3 levels of image noise and 3 levels of action noise.
Instance segmentation: compares SOLOv2 (ResNet34), BlendMask (DLA34), YOLACT++ and Mask R-CNN (Detectron2/MMdetection). SOLOv2 is chosen for speed and mAP@0.5 (BlendMask is better on mAP@0.5:0.95).

Control-based SLAM (CDXSLAM / OpenVSLAM variant): replaces the constant-velocity motion model with the velocity matrix V = C_i^-1 from the expected action displacement (forward d, rotate ±α, stop). Keypoint matching is done by projection, which is faster than Bag of Words.

Hierarchical RL: two-level policy based on Hierarchical Actor-Critic. The high level (TD3) outputs a subgoal coordinate near the agent, and the low level (DDDQN) outputs forward/left/right actions. The state includes depth, a semantic mask filtered to the goal class, and localization.
Hindsight training: hindsight action and hindsight goal transitions (HER-like) with sparse binary reward (0 on subgoal reached, otherwise -1), avoiding manual reward shaping.

Real-time deployment: modules profiled on a V100 server and on a Clearpath Husky with a ZED camera and GTX1050Ti. SOLOv2 runs at about 15 fps on the robot and 55 fps on the server, and the policy at 111 fps on the robot and 200 fps on the server.

setting.backbone: SOLOv2-ResNet34 (trained), CDXSLAM (HF-Net + tracking), TD3 + DDDQN hierarchical policy (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: HISNav Dataset (135,962 Habitat/Matterport3D images from 49 scenes, noise-augmented) for segmentation and SLAM; RL trained in Habitat on a single scene with multiple episodes
setting.observation: RGB-D images (640x320) plus SLAM pose estimate
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: stay, turn left α, turn right α, forward d; high level outputs a continuous subgoal coordinate
setting.privileged: none at test time (the scene map is used only for visualization; the goal object coordinates are used for reward only during training)

numbers_note: The object navigation and point navigation RL results are given only in figures (SPL curves, Figures 10 and 11), and the text states only approximate values (SPL about 0.6-0.7). No official-benchmark tables. The tables for segmentation mAP and SLAM errors were not legible in the extracted text.
results: SOLOv2 gives the best quality/speed trade-off for segmentation (about 15 fps on the robot). Control-integrated CDXSLAM and OpenVSLAM improve both relative and absolute errors. On noisy point-goal navigation the hierarchical agent reaches SPL 0.6 in 3M steps versus 6M for PPO and RND, and converges to about 0.7, the same as both baselines. Object-navigation SPL is described as low and only a training curve on one scene is shown.
limitations: Object navigation was evaluated only on a single training scene with figure-only results and no standard benchmark comparison; SPL is admittedly low.
The neural-network SLAM (CDXSLAM) often loses tracking on noisy data because its keypoint network was not trained with such noise.
The system depends on known expected action displacements and simulation-trained models; sim2real is shown only qualitatively through trajectories on a campus.
